title: Ohio Floods
change_caption: Red: brighter in the BEFORE image. Cyan: brighter in the AFTER image. Gray/white: little change. Black: no data. This compares image brightness, not a measured flood extent.

radar_explainer.what_radar_sees: Calm open water reflects the radar signal away from the satellite and looks dark, while flooded vegetation or buildings can bounce it back strongly and look bright. Radar also works through clouds and rain, which is why it is useful during storms.
radar_explainer.polarization_note: The product contains HH and HV channels. The quicklook image does not tell us which channel it displays, so we make no polarization claim for this view.

question: What caused this change on Earth's surface?
hints: Switch to the Radar Difference view: it highlights where the radar signal changed the most.
Heavy rain fell over a short time here, the kind of storm that can push creeks and rivers out of their banks.

story.summary: On August 19-20, 2026, heavy thunderstorms dropped several inches of rain on parts of Ohio. The National Weather Service in Wilmington reported 3 to 6 inches in Shelby and Logan counties and 4 to 7 inches in the heaviest areas of Franklin and Licking counties. Local media reported more than a dozen swift-water rescues.
story.nisar_insight: Water changes how radar signal bounces back, so a flooded area can look different from the same place on a dry day. NISAR's radar also works through clouds and rain, so it can image the ground during the storms that cause floods. Here, a before image (17 July) and an after image (22 August) are compared.
story.looking_forward: Because radar sees through clouds and rain, it is valuable when optical satellites are blind. With a revisit of about 12 days, a single NISAR pass can miss the flood peak, so future flood mapping would combine NISAR with other satellites and ground reports.

decision.scenario: You're coordinating emergency response as the floodwaters rise. Using the radar change map, where do you focus your limited water-rescue teams first?

choices.text: The areas showing the strongest radar signal change
choices.feedback: A sensible start. Strong radar change over low-lying land can point to standing water, so it helps decide where to look first. It does not show water depth or where people are stranded, so teams still need field reports to confirm.

choices.text: The town centers, regardless of what the radar shows
choices.feedback: Population centers matter, but ignoring the radar data risks missing flooded rural areas where people can be just as stranded. Combining both is the stronger approach.

choices.text: Wait until the rain fully stops to send teams
choices.feedback: Waiting costs valuable time during a flood. Radar can see through rain, but NISAR passes only about every 12 days, so the first response relies on emergency calls and field reports while satellite data helps with planning and mapping.

caveat: Visual comparison of quicklook images, not a validated flood extent map. The two acquisitions are 36 days apart (17 July and 22 August), so some of the visible change may come from normal seasonal changes in vegetation or soil moisture. The after image was taken 2-3 days after the storm, so some floodwater may already have drained. The scene covers west-central Ohio; the heaviest-rain areas around Franklin and Licking counties lie outside it.
